Mr. Jyotirmoy Barua, Advocate ------ For the Accused-Petitioner. 
Mr. Muhammad Amirul Haq, Advocates ------ For the Complainant-opposite party.
parties:
PHILIP GAIN
VS.
THE STATE AND ANOTHER
full_judgment:
Borhanuddin, J: This rule has been issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the proceedings of C. R. Case no. 5734 of 2008 under sections 420/190/109 of the Penal Code, now pending in the Court of learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Facts relevant for disposal of the rule are that opposite party no.2 herein as complainant lodged a petition of complaint in the court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka, contending inter alia that the complainant is a driver employed in the Society for Environment and Human Development (SHED), a non government organization; Accused no.1 is the Director of SHED and accused nos. 2 and 3 are Co-ordinator and Chief Accountant respectively of the organization; On 01.07.2005, accused no. 1, his mother and sister were going to Gopalgonj by a private car belonged to the organization; Complainant was in the driving seat; While their car crossed Dauladia Ferry ghat, accused no.1 wished to drive the car; Complainant tried to resist him but the accused insisted and started driving by taking the key; The car confront a serious accident at Faridpur Munshi Bazar and mother of the accused died at the Faridpur Medical College Hospital due to severe head injury; Complainant also sustained serious injury; A General Diary lodged on 01.07.2005 with the Faridpur Kotwali Police Station; Complainant tried to lodge FIR regarding the accident but the accused and other persons promised to compensate him and also threatened him not to file any case; On 02.08.2015, accused no.1 in presence of other witnesses agreed to pay taka 5,00,000/- (Five lacs) to the complainant as compensation and. bear medical expenses of the complainant and also provide full paid leave and other facilities entitled in his service; On 25.08.2008, the accused’s in connivance with one another served notice upon the complainant terminating his service; Complainant tried to meet the accused no.1 but failed rather accused no. 1 instructed his employees accused nos. 2 and 3 to take signature of the complainant on a plain paper; Complainant apprehends that they tried to procure his signature to prevent him from claiming compensation and filing complaint petition; Complainant went to the Mohammadpur Police Station to lodge ejahar but police refused to register his case as such this petition of complaint; The petition of complainant is registered as Petition Case No.5734 of 2008. 

 4. The complainant again filed naraji against the said police report and upon hearing learned Magistrate directed the Deputy Commissioner, Detective Branch, Dhaka Metropolitan police to investigate the matter with an officer not below the rank of Inspector vide order dated 27.06.2011. A senior Assistant Police Commissioner of Detective Branch, Dhaka Metropolitan Police, further investigated the case and after completing the investigation submitted report on 26.09.2011 in the court below stating that during investigation police has examined as many as six witnesses and recorded their statement under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but found no substance of the allegation and the complainant failed to produce any evidence in support of his allegation that the accused promised to pay taka 5,00,000/- (five lacs) to him. It is also stated in the report that the accused no.1 had treated the complainant at Faridpur Medical College Hospital and later on at Shomorita Hospital, Dhaka and the organization bore all medical expenses. Again the complainant filed naraji on 07.02.2012 against police report and the learned Magistrate again ordered the Deputy Commissioner, Detective Branch, to investigate the matter with another police officer. Accordingly, a Senior Assistant Police Commissioner of Crime Investigation Department further investigated the matter and after investigation submitted his report on 10.7.2012 in the court below with a finding that the allegation has no basis. On 19.11.2012 the complainant filed naraji against the said report. Upon hearing, learned Chief Metropolitan Magistrate allowed the application and directed the learned Metropolitan Magistrate to conduct a judicial inquiry vide order dated 28.01.2013. After inquiry, learned Magistrate submitted the report on 12.03.2013. On the basis of the report, learned Metropolitan Magistrate took cognizance against the accused’s under section 420 of the Penal Code vide order dated 30.04.2013. 

 6. At this stage, accused no.1 as petitioner preferred instant criminal miscellaneous case by filing an application under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained the present rule along with an order of stay. 

 7. Mr. Jyotirmoy Barua, learned advocate appearing for the accused-petitioner submits that high ranking officials of the police department including detective branch and criminal investigation department investigated the matter four times as directed by the court below and all the time after inquiry submitted report holding that allegation has no basis but the court below without considering record of the case framed charge mechanically in contravention of the provisions of sections 241A and 242 of the Code of Criminal Procedure as such criminal proceeding is liable to be quashed. He also submits that admittedly mother of the accused petitioner died in the accident and sister of the accused petitioner along with complainant were injured as such it is evident that the occurrence was an accident but the court below without considering this factual aspect framed charge against the accused petitioner as such criminal proceeding is liable to be quashed. He again submits that allegation made in the petition of complaint even if accepted as true do not constitute any offence of criminal breach of trust punishable under section 406 or cheating punishable under section 420 of the Penal Code as such criminal proceeding is a sheer abuse of the process of the Court and liable to be quashed. He further submits that the court below while framing charge did not consider the broad probability of the case, total effect of the evidence and documents produced before the court as such the proceeding is liable to be quashed. 

 8. On the other hand, Mr. Md. Amirul Huq learned advocate appearing for the opposite party no.2 submits that the court below after considering record of the case found ingredient to frame charge against the accused’s as such the rule is liable to be discharged. He also submits that in the judicial inquiry learned magistrate found substance of the allegation as such court below rightly and legally framed charge against the accused. 

 241A. When the accused appears or is brought before the Magistrate, and if the Magistrate, upon consideration of the record of the case and the documents submitted therewith and making such examination, if any, of the accused as the Magistrate thinks necessary and after giving the prosecution and the accused an opportunity of being heard, considers the charge to be groundless, he shall discharge the accused and record his reasons for so doing. 

 13. Section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure contemplates consideration of record of the case, documents submitted, examination of accused and hearing prosecution and the accused. The learned Magistrate has to conclude the exercise under section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure and lie may either discharge the accused with reasoning or may reject the application for discharge with reasoning. After conclusion of the exercise under section 241A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Magistrate will embark upon his judicial responsibility under section 242 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to frame charge. Whether it will be in the same sitting or the same date is a matter of convenience and practice of the Magistrate. 

 16. In several cases Indian Supreme Court observed that: 

 "In exercising jurisdiction under section 227 of the Code the Judge cannot act merely as a Post Office or a mouthpiece of the prosecution, but has to consider the broad probabilities of the case, the total effect of the evidence and the documents produced before the court, any basic infirmities appearing in the case and so on. This however does not mean that the judge should make a roving enquiry into the pros and cons of the matter and weigh the evidence as if he was conducting a trial.” 

 17. In the case of State of Karnataka-Vs- L. Muniswamy and others, reported in (1977) 2 SCC 699, Indian Supreme Court observed that: 

 "The High Court therefore is entitled to go into the reasons given by the Sessions Judge in support of his order and to determine for itself whether the order is justified by the facts and circumstances of the case. Section 482 of the New Code, which corresponds to Section 561-A of the Code of 1898, provides that: Nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or affect the inherent powers of the High Court to make such orders as may be necessary to give effect to any order under this Code or to prevent abuse of the process of any Court or other wise to secure the ends of justice. 

 In the exercise of this wholesome power, the High Court is entitled to quash a proceeding if it comes to the conclusion that allowing the proceeding to continue would be an abuse of the process of the Court or that the ends of justice require that the proceeding ought to be quashed. The saving of the High Court's inherent powers, both in civil and criminal matters, is designed to achieve a salutary public purpose which is that a court proceeding ought not to be permitted to degenerate into a weapon of harassment or persecution. In a criminal case, the veiled object behind a lame prosecution, the very nature of the material on which the structure of the prosecution rests and the like would justify the High Court in quashing the proceeding in the interest of justice. The ends of justice are higher than the ends of mere law though justice has got to be administered according to laws made by the legislature. The compelling necessity for making these observations is that without a proper realisation of the object and purpose of the provision which seeks to save the inherent powers of the High Court to do justice between the State and its subjects, it would be impossible to appreciate the width and contours of that salient jurisdiction." 

 18. It is apparent that the facts and circumstances of the case in hand are distinct and different. High ranking police officials investigated the matter four times pursuant to court's order. We have also gone through statement of the witnesses recorded in the judicial inquiry and report of the learned Judicial Magistrate. However, we do not like to enter into the pros and cons of the merit of the case. But we are of the opinion that the charge framing order dated 08.12.2013 is not in compliance with the provisions of sections 241A and 242 of the Code of Criminal Procedure with reasons to form opinion by the Magistrate. As such, we are inclined to quash order dated 08.12.2013 passed by the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Court No.31, Dhaka, and also directed the learned Magistrate to dispose of the application under section 241 A of the Code of Criminal Procedure filed by the accused petitioner in compliance with the respective provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure in the light of observations made above.
